Rémy Cointreau (RCO-FR): a good brand business at trough earnings, whose causes for concern are clearing, on a multiple that has already recovered half-way

Triaging A&J Memo

Data as at 23 November 2026; share price €50.35. Money in euros. The fiscal year ends on 31 March (FY27 is the year to 31 March 2027). Earnings per share are on the brokers' adjusted basis unless stated.

#0 The investment case

The verdict in brief
  • The fundamentals are skewed to the upside. Earnings are at a trough, four causes for concern are clearing on dated evidence, and consensus gives the €100m RC Forward plan almost no net credit.
  • The share price is roughly balanced. The two-year forward multiple has already risen from 14.9 to 22.6 times, so the market has paid for part of the recovery.
  • The expected return is moderate: about +11% over 18 months, probability-weighted, with +54% in the better case and (19)% in the worse case.
  • Two questions decide whether the return is about 10% a year or much more: whether cognac price-mix stops falling, and how much of RC Forward's savings the company keeps. Both are tested on known dates between January and June 2027.

1. The one idea: Rémy's profit is price-mix multiplied by shipments, less a largely fixed cost base. Rémy Cointreau is a cognac house with a liqueur business attached. Cognac is 61% of sales and about 77% of operating profit, and the US and China together take roughly 60-70% of sales and over 80% of profit. The company buys eaux-de-vie (the distilled wine that ages into cognac) under multi-year contracts, ages them for years (inventory of €2.2bn, 2.3 times sales) and sells through wholesalers at a 66% gross margin, against costs that are largely fixed and in euros.

Three consequences follow from that business model:

  • The competitive position. Protected origin, aged stock and Louis XIII are real barriers to entry, but the same locked-in stock turns a dip in demand into discounting across the industry.
  • The main risk. Wholesalers build and run down their stock, so shipments can recover while prices keep falling.
  • The sensitivity. In FY26 organic sales rose 0.2%, yet operating profit fell 11.5%.

2. The change: four causes for concern are clearing at the same time, so the profit base is being rebuilt from several directions at once.

Inside the company, a new chief executive has changed the pricing doctrine and launched a large cost plan. Since June 2025 the new chief executive has dropped the doctrine of price before volume and launched RC Forward, a plan worth about €100m of gross value by FY2028-29. That gross value equals 60% of FY26 operating profit, but only 10% of it arrives in FY27.

The headwinds are equally specific, and most of them act on price. Cognac price-mix fell 8.3% in the first quarter of FY27 and 4% in the second. Hennessy has cut prices and is spending to regain share. The cognac industry holds about ten years of stock. Sales to consumers in China during the Mid-Autumn Festival missed plan, so wholesalers there will destock in the third quarter. The forces lifting volume and cutting cost are strong; the forces acting on price are still negative.

3. How the change reaches the financials: through volume first, costs second, and not through price. Volume comes first, as shipments catch up with depletions and, from April 2027, as a US cognac priced below VSOP reaches the market. Costs come second, with the bulk of RC Forward's savings in FY28 and FY29. On my forecasts, sales grow 3.7% in FY27 and 5.5% in each of FY28 and FY29, the EBITDA margin rises from 22.5% to 24.1%, and earnings per share rise from €1.71 in FY26 to €1.75, €1.96 and €2.22. That is growth of 12-13% a year from FY28, within 3% of consensus.

The arithmetic behind that forecast is the most useful single insight in this memo. Sales about €144m higher by FY29, at a contribution margin near 46%, add about €66m of operating profit. Three years of cost inflation take back about €24m. The net €42m is close to the €47m of operating profit growth I forecast and the €49m in consensus. Consensus therefore pays almost nothing, net, for a plan worth €100m gross: it assumes the savings are reinvested or lost to falling price-mix.

FY27 guidance looks safe; the real test is the FY28 guidance in June 2027. Sell-side estimates have risen 4-6% in six months, almost entirely because of currency. The brokers' narrative has moved from "structural decline" to "tentative recovery", yet only 23% of brokers rate the shares a Buy.

4. The foundation: the brands and barriers are sound, but the financial profile is not. Return on capital employed is 7.7%, cash conversion is far below peers', and pricing power in the middle of the range is demonstrably impaired: US VSOP volumes recover only at shelf prices below $49.99. Management is untested in spirits but has started credibly, with three results releases in line or better since the reset and €230m of costs removed in the two years before it. The longer record is poor: estimates fell more than 80% in four years, and the company withdrew its 2030 targets. The foundation therefore supports a recovery in volume and cost, but does not yet support a return to the old operating margin of 25-28%.

5. The setup: a cause for concern clearing in a quality cyclical at trough earnings, with only one of the two troughs present. The best fit among the standard setups is 'CfC in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough, leading to reversion to normal' (CfC: cause for concern; trough-on-trough: trough earnings on a trough multiple). RC Forward adds an element of 'Big Corporate Change-driven EPSU' (earnings-per-share upgrades driven by major corporate change).

  • Present: trough earnings (sales 40% and earnings per share about 70% below the FY23 peak), named causes for concern clearing on dated evidence, brand quality, and a quantified self-help plan.
  • Missing: the second trough, a trough multiple, because the two-year forward multiple is 22.6 times against a low of 14.9 times in March 2025 and the share price is 49% above its 52-week low; an agreed "normal" level of earnings to revert to; and a stated net value for RC Forward.

6. The reward and the skew: the fundamentals are skewed to the upside, but the share price is roughly balanced. The skew in the fundamentals is positive because the earnings base is low and consensus gives RC Forward no net credit. The skew in the share price is roughly balanced because the re-rating from 15 to 23 times has already paid for the causes for concern clearing.

In the better case (a depletion-led US restock, flat price-mix and about a quarter of RC Forward kept), two-year forward earnings per share in 18 months are about €2.85, and at 27 times the shares are worth about €77: a return of about +54% with the dividend. In the worse case (the restock fades, price-mix keeps falling and currency reverses), €2.10 at 19 times gives €40, a return of about (19)%, and the bears' floor arguments sit lower still, at €21-26 a share. My base case returns +15%. Weighting the better, base and worse cases at 20%, 45% and 35% gives an 18-month return of about +11%. At the guideline fair multiple of 32.5 times, the base-case earnings would give +64%, but I think the guideline multiple needs proof that this business cannot yet offer.

7. What has to be true: three conditions, each tested on known dates between November 2026 and June 2027.

The five judgements that move the value of the shares most

  1. How much of RC Forward is kept. Each €10m of operating profit kept is worth €10m × (1 − 28.5% tax) ÷ 53.0m shares = €0.135 a share, or 6% of my FY29 earnings per share of €2.22. Keeping 30% of the plan (€30m) adds €0.40 a share, or 18%. Bernstein's forecast of €68m of operating profit growth to FY29, against my €47m, adds €0.28 a share, or 13%.
  2. Cognac price-mix. Cognac sales are about €620m. If cognac price-mix is four points worse than I forecast in FY28 and three-quarters of the shortfall drops to profit, operating profit falls by €620m × 4% × 75% = €18.6m: €0.25 a share, or 13% of FY28 earnings per share of €1.96. Two such years would take about 22% off FY29 earnings per share.
  3. The US restock. Sales growth three points lower in FY28 (2.5% instead of 5.5%) means €31m less sales; at a 46% contribution margin that is €14m less operating profit, €0.19 a share, or about 10% of FY28 earnings per share.
  4. Currency. On the company's rule, one cent on the euro-dollar rate moves operating profit by €2m. Five cents is €10m, or €0.135 a share, 7% of FY28 earnings per share; a 10% move in the dollar is worth about €0.31 a share. FY27 is 65-70% hedged, so the currency exposure starts in FY28.
  5. The multiple. In 18 months, two-year forward earnings per share on my forecasts are €2.53, so each turn of the multiple is worth €2.53 a share, or 5% of today's price. The gap between today's 22.6 times and the guideline 32.5 times is 9.8 turns, worth €25 a share, or half of today's price. The multiple therefore outweighs any single earnings judgement above.

Scorecard

#1 Operating environment

Inference: the tailwinds are one-off steps in the level of sales, not lasting growth rates. Our own Sector Digest makes the same point: a destocking that ends lifts reported sales without any growth in consumption. The US step is mostly still ahead, because US shipments are running below depletions during the distributor change. The China step was partly taken early, in the second quarter, and some of it will be given back in the third. FY27 and FY28 therefore collect the steps, and from FY29 the case needs consumers to drink more cognac or pay more for it.

The counter-case, tested: the bear case has narrowed since June. The Risks report of June 2026 concluded that the "no recovery" and "false friend" readings fitted the evidence best. Several items that the report treated as diagnostic have since moved in the company's favour: the tariff cost (€20m then, about €5m now), US depletions ((4)% then, about flat now), leverage (eased by the hybrid bond) and currency. What remains of the bear case is narrower and sharper: price erosion, the industry's stock, and savings that arrive late.

What would change my view. Two consecutive quarters of US cognac depletions falling by a mid-single-digit percentage; China withdrawing the price undertaking; or a stronger euro.

Against the market: I read the tariff and currency relief as risk removed, not as profit spent. I agree with consensus that the environment has stabilised rather than recovered. Where I differ is that the market reads the tariff and currency relief as profit that the company then "spent"; I read it as risk removed, which matters more for the multiple than for earnings. The wider market backdrop is mixed for this stock: our weekly digest favours staples and beverages, but not France, fragile companies or momentum, and the present market de-rates a leveraged defensive stock with contested estimates.

Conclusion: the environment has turned from hostile to neutral, with dated relief on stock levels, tariffs and currency, but with price still falling. Bearing on the case: the environment supports step 2 (the change) for FY27 and FY28, and leaves open whether demand carries the case beyond the restock.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. The external positives are steps rather than growth rates: US and China destocking ending (US wholesaler stock about four months, NABCA volumes +1%), China's 38% duty replaced by a price undertaking, tariff cost down from EUR 20m to about 5m and currency flipped to a EUR 3-5m gain, set against price falling on 91% of US products, Hennessy cutting price with about ten years of industry stock, substitution by tequila and RTD, and a bankrupt US distributor; price counts as well as volume, so the balance is only a mild net positive for FY27-28 with nothing structural beyond the restock. Consensus sales growth at the 54th percentile agrees, so it sits just above Kerry's neutral environment and below OEM's modestly positive one.

#2 Corporate change

Evidence: RC Forward is one part of a broad reorganisation. RC Forward has five levers (distribution, revenue growth management, advertising efficiency, central procurement and a simpler organisation), a Chief Transformation Officer, and a steering committee of five functions reporting to the chief executive. Around the plan, the company has created a Prestige division for Louis XIII; set up an Emerging Markets unit under a hire from Pernod Ricard, with a goal of doubling its sales in three years; appointed a Group Chief Markets Officer over all regions and new heads of Rémy Martin and of North America; exited low-margin partner brands; cut capital spending to €37m; cut eaux-de-vie purchases by 20% after earlier cuts of 25-45%; and declared itself open to selling brands ("no sacred cows").

Inference: the most valuable internal change is the new pricing doctrine, not the cost plan. Under the old doctrine, the company raised US VSOP prices more than 30% above pre-pandemic levels while Hennessy cut its prices, and Rémy Martin's US VSOP volumes fell 28%. The new doctrine has already turned Rémy Martin from a share loser into a share gainer (up 0.6 points in the US in FY26 and three points in China in 2025), at the cost of mix. RC Forward is best read as the funding for that volume strategy. That reading explains why brokers give the plan little net credit, and why the company reinvested the whole of this year's tariff saving. It also explains the positive skew: any part of the plan not needed to fund lower prices is a pure gain.

Problems and risks: the agenda is wide for a small organisation. About 1,800 people are running a wide agenda. Former executives describe friction between Paris and the US. The chief executive left his previous post before the results of his plan there were visible. The launch of a cheaper cognac could dilute the Rémy Martin brand that the launch is meant to recruit drinkers for.

The counter-case. Redburn expects competition to absorb every euro that RC Forward saves, leaving the operating margin at 19-22% in 2030.

What would change my view. Upward: a stated reinvestment rate, or savings running well ahead of the 10% of the plan due in year one. Downward: senior departures in the US, or the April 2027 launch taking volume from VSOP.

Against the market: I share consensus's base case, but see a better range of outcomes around it. In my base case I agree with consensus that RC Forward brings no net benefit. I differ on the range around that base case: the company has shown it can take cost out, so the uncertainty is how much of the saving it chooses to spend, and that choice becomes easier as price-mix stabilises.

Conclusion: the internal change is real, sensibly sequenced and, on cost, demonstrably within the company's abilities, but its net value is unstated. Bearing on the case: it supports step 2, it is the main source of positive skew in step 6, and step 3 stays open until the company gives a reinvestment rate.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. A new chief executive has replaced price-before-volume (already turning Remy into a share gainer, +0.6 points US, +3 points China) and launched RC Forward, EUR 100m gross or 60% of FY26 operating profit, with a transformation office, a Prestige division, an Emerging Markets unit, capex and eaux-de-vie purchases cut and the balance sheet repaired with a hybrid, after EUR 230m of costs already removed; but only 10% of the plan lands in FY27, its net value is unstated and largely reinvested in price, the CEO is untested in spirits and a cheaper cognac could dilute VSOP. This is a complete, funded, multi-part self-help programme that so far repairs a cyclical business rather than extending it, so it sits just below OEM's working change of control and above Odfjell's incremental positives.

#3 Business, industry and management foundations

Industry structure: the industry is closed to entrants, but it is also hard to exit. Four houses hold about 90% of cognac sales, appellation rules and the years of ageing required keep new entrants out, and brand owners capture most of the value (gross margins near 70% in stable periods). Against that, the top five US distributors hold two-thirds of the US market, and the aged-inventory model is a barrier to exit as well as to entry: eaux-de-vie purchase contracts run for years, so a glut cannot be cut quickly and turns into a price war.

Competitive position: Rémy's moat is deep at the top of the range and shallow in the middle. Louis XIII has more than three-quarters of spirits sold above $1,000 a bottle, and the company is strong in China's higher price tiers. In US VSOP, where much of the profit swing sits, Hennessy sells about four times Rémy Martin's volume and consumer loyalty is weak. The industry's profit pool has shifted towards the part of the range where Rémy's moat is weakest.

Financial profile: Rémy is below its peers on every measure except forecast growth. The table below sets out the gaps in margin, cash flow, leverage and working capital. Only the consensus growth from here is above the peers', and that growth is the gift of a low base. Two details matter in reading the table: the company's own measure of free cash flow was €54m in FY26, helped by the timing of payables, and the company's own measure of leverage was 3.2 times EBITDA before the hybrid bond.

Management and culture: plain-spoken and patient, but unproven in spirits. The chief executive, Franck Marilly, brings 30 years in luxury goods and none in spirits. Luca Marotta, finance chief since 2013 and now deputy chief executive, carries the institutional memory and is a key-person risk. Communication has become plainer: management now admits that pricing power cannot be guaranteed. The family holds a majority of the capital and about two-thirds or more of the votes (the reports give slightly different figures). Family control brings patience, shown by the 76.8% take-up of the dividend in shares, and removes outside pressure. No insider has bought Rémy shares in the market, whereas Pernod Ricard's chief executive and Diageo's chair have bought shares in their own companies.

The counter-case: quality is depressed by the cycle, not impaired. After the 2012-14 China downturn, margins recovered within a year through price-mix and cost.

What would change my view. Two half-years of positive cognac price-mix would show that the middle of the range has repaired.

Against the market: the premium multiple mostly reflects trough earnings, not quality. The market reads Rémy's two-year forward multiple of 22.6 times, against 11.8 times for Pernod Ricard and 13.6 times for Diageo, as a quality premium. I think the premium mostly reflects trough earnings, and should be judged that way.

Conclusion: strong brands in a closed industry, on a financial profile that is currently below average, run by a management team that is promising but unproven. Bearing on the case: the foundations weaken step 4, because they support reversion in volume and cost but not yet in price or margin.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. The industry is closed (four houses hold about 90% of cognac, appellation and ageing barriers) and Louis XIII is a fortress, but the aged-stock model turns any glut into a price war, US distributors are concentrated, and the moat is shallow in US VSOP where the profit swing sits; management is promising but unproven and predictability is low. The financial profile is weak today (ROIC 3.1%, 23rd percentile; ROE 18th; negative free cash flow; net debt/EBITDA 3.5x, worse than 80%; 645 days of working capital) and new capital in ageing stock earns below its cost while price-mix falls, though the 83rd-percentile gross margin shows the brand value, so it sits just below Shell's cyclical-depressed quality and level with Xvivo's genuine moat inside weak current returns.

#4 Guidance and delivery record

Evidence: FY27 guidance is modest, and October's windfalls were not added to it. FY27 guidance is a return to organic sales growth (already 2.9% at the half-year) and a slight organic gain in margin. When two windfalls arrived in October (tariffs €15m better, currency €8-13m better), management raised neither the sales objective nor the profit objective: it reinvested the tariff saving and let brokers add the currency gain. The first three results under the new plan were in line or ahead: the FY26 results, first-quarter FY27 organic sales growth of +1.3% against +0.3% expected, and second-quarter growth of +4.2% against about 3.5% expected. Before those three, the record was one of misses: a guidance cut in October 2025, the withdrawal of the 33% margin target for 2030, and a long-term share plan that vested at only 51%.

Inference: the new team sets a low bar and spends what comes in above it. That habit makes guidance reliable and upgrades to guidance rare. Upgrades to sell-side forecasts will therefore come from sales beats and currency, not from the company lifting its margin objective. The habit showed in June 2026, when the first FY27 guidance led Deutsche Bank to write that the guidance implied a downgrade. I expect the FY28 guidance in June 2027 to be set in the same way.

The counter-case. The recent beats were against a bar lowered by 80%, and both quarterly beats were driven by shipments. Historically, wholesaler stock, not management, has decided whether the company hit or missed.

What would change my view. A profit objective raised during the year, or a medium-term target with a stated margin.

Against the market. Brokers describe the guidance as "deliberately modest", and I agree. I would add that modest guidance combined with reinvested windfalls is evidence of weak pricing power as much as of prudence.

Conclusion: guidance is conservative and currently credible, set by a team with three good results behind it and a long corporate record of misses behind that. Bearing on the case: the record supports step 3 on meeting guidance and weakens step 3 on raising it.

Score: 44, set by the Rater. Current guidance is deliberately modest and has been met or beaten at three prints since the reset (Q1 organic +1.3% vs +0.3% expected, Q2 +4.2% vs about 3.5%), but inside the last two to three years guidance was cut (October 2025), the 33% 2030 margin target was withdrawn, estimates fell over 80% in four years and the share plan vested at 51%, and the habit of reinvesting windfalls means guidance is rarely raised. A recent severe miss followed by beats against a lowered bar places it beside Instalco and just below Sdiptech's untested new targets.

#5 Earnings gearing

Operating leverage: earnings are twice as sensitive to price as to volume, and price is the variable in the worst shape. On an FY28 base, 1% more volume adds about 2.4% to operating profit and 3.3% to earnings per share, while 1% more price adds about 5.3% and 7%. Morgan Stanley's older rule of thumb makes the same point from the other side: a 12% fall in sales has historically cut operating profit by 25-30%.

Financial leverage: earnings per share move about 1.3 times as fast as operating profit. Interest and the hybrid coupon together take about a quarter of operating profit in FY28. The hybrid coupon itself is €16.9m a year, or €0.32 a share before tax relief and before the interest saved on the debt that the hybrid replaced; Morgan Stanley puts the net cost at 2-3% of earnings from FY28.

Pricing power: negative at present, and elastic. Developed-market spirits volumes respond to targeted price cuts at a ratio of about two to one, and the $49.99 shelf price for VSOP is a hard threshold.

Cost scope: proven (see step 4 of #0), with procurement the largest lever in RC Forward. Lower eaux-de-vie purchases also release cash: Bernstein expects cash conversion to improve as the old purchase contracts roll off.

Feedback loops: a favourable volume loop and an adverse discounting loop run in opposite directions, and the industry's ten years of stock keep the adverse loop turning.

So what: revenue growth produces outsized profit growth only when price-mix is flat. The first half of FY27 brought the other kind of growth: cognac volume rose about 16% while cognac price-mix fell 4-8%. The gross margin in the 25 November results will show how much of that volume reached profit; my files cannot say.

The counter-case and what would change my view. If the US launch below VSOP widens the price ladder without pulling VSOP prices down, mix stabilises and the gearing works in the company's favour; a cognac price-mix reading near zero would tell me so.

Against the market. Bulls cite "massive operating leverage", and bears cite margin dilution. Both are right, about different variables, and I think the market under-uses the distinction between volume gearing and price gearing.

Conclusion: the business has high operating gearing and moderate financial gearing, and its earnings are twice as sensitive to price as to volume. Bearing on the case: the gearing supports step 3 in mechanism, and makes the price-mix condition in step 7 the one that decides how much of the growth becomes profit.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. The structure has strong fixed-cost gearing (66% gross margin on a largely fixed euro cost base: 1% of volume adds about 2.4% to operating profit, 1% of price about 5.3%; a 12% sales fall historically cut profit 25-30%), proven cost-out scope (EUR 230m removed, RC Forward procurement) and financial leverage taking EPS to about 1.3x operating profit, and consensus EPS grows about 2.4 times revenue against a median of 2. But the most geared lever, pricing, is negative and elastic (the $49.99 VSOP line) with an adverse discount loop fed by industry stock, and the leverage is stretched rather than comfortable, so two gears are proven and the third works against it: below the 75 level, well above ordinary.

Is there double-digit growth? Yes, from FY28. Earnings per share compound at 12.5% a year from FY27 to FY30. FY27 itself is a base year, with growth of 2%.

Is the forecast better than the past? It is plainly better than the last three years, but not better than the longer past. FY31 sales would still be below FY24's, the FY31 EBITDA margin of 25% compares with 29% in FY24 on the same basis, and FY31 earnings per share of €2.71 compare with €3.86 in FY24. Four tests fixed the forecasts.

Where I sit against consensus: slightly below, for financing reasons rather than operating ones. My operating profit is 1-2% below consensus in FY27-29, and my earnings per share are level with consensus in FY27 and 2-3% below in FY28-29. The gap comes more from the hybrid coupon and financing costs, which my files suggest brokers treat unevenly, than from a different operating view. I can name no evidence that the sell-side lacks, so I have not forecast above consensus.

The counter-case and what would change my view. Bernstein's path would put FY29 earnings about 13% higher; Redburn's would put the margin two to four points lower. A stated reinvestment rate would move me towards Bernstein; another year of (4)% price-mix would move me towards Redburn.

Conclusion: double-digit earnings growth from FY28, on forecasts at or just under consensus, with margins recovering only part of the way to their past level. Bearing on the case: the forecasts support step 3 in direction and size, and show that the case does not need forecasts above consensus to work, only for consensus to be met.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. Growth in the 10-15% band gives B, but I place it at the floor of the band: it is a recovery from a trough (EPS still well below FY24's 3.86), the EBITDA margin climbs only to about 25% against 29% in FY24, and on the brokers' FY26 base it sits on the 10% cut-off, although the growth is organic and in line with consensus.

#7 Scope for upgrades

Upgrades have to come from items that neither guidance nor consensus yet includes. Counting only those items:

Not in consensus, positive. (1) Any net benefit from RC Forward, the largest item. (2) The size of the US restock once shipments reach depletions; part of the restock is already in the 6% sales growth that consensus has for FY28. (3) A US tariff rate of 10% in FY28, worth a few million euros if the company does not reinvest it. (4) The US tariff refund, which is cash but will sit outside adjusted earnings. (5) Proceeds from any brand sale.

Not in consensus, negative. (1) The third-quarter stock adjustment in China. (2) The hybrid coupon, which some brokers have yet to deduct. (3) Price-mix staying negative into FY28. (4) FY28 guidance set low in June 2027.

My judgement of each event over the next 18 months is in the table below (dates after November 2026 are estimated from last year's calendar).

Reading the table: the odds of upgrades tilt positive only from mid-2027. Over the next six months the odds of upgrades and downgrades are about even, with the January sales release the weakest point. From mid-2027 the odds tilt positive, provided the restock and the savings arrive together. Over the whole 18 months, I put a 40% chance on FY29 consensus earnings ending at least 5% higher than today, 30% on them ending within 5% of today, and 30% on them ending at least 5% lower.

The counter-case and what would change my view. A profit objective raised on 25 November, or third-quarter sales that absorb the China destock without turning negative, would bring the positive tilt forward by two quarters.

Against the market. The upgrades of the last six months are momentum, and they came from currency. The market may be extrapolating them; I do not, because nothing in my files tells me where the euro goes next.

Conclusion: the scope for upgrades is real but back-loaded, and over the next 6-12 months it is not unusually skewed to the positive. Bearing on the case: it leaves step 3 open on timing, and it is the main reason the 18-month reward in step 6 is moderate.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is most likely met rather than raised at the next events (about 80% met on FY27) and the FY28 guidance in June 2027 is likelier set below consensus (35%) than above (20%), given the team's habit of reinvesting windfalls; consensus FY28-29 is about even over six months with the January China destock and the hybrid coupon as known negatives against the unpriced net value of RC Forward and a lower US tariff, and the narrative is turning to valuation (Bernstein downgrade, median target below the price). With roughly flat expected revisions against 5% revenue growth (about the 40th percentile) and the positive tilt only after mid-2027, it sits just above Tele2 and below Kerry.

#8 Current momentum

Guidance: only the currency and tariff components were upgraded in October 2026; the operating objectives were not.

Sell-side momentum: estimates are rising, and the pinned grade is B (dashboard of 22-23 November 2026). Consensus earnings per share for FY28 (the year to March 2028) are up 4% over one month, 5% over three months and 6% over six months, though still 9% lower than a year ago. Average target prices are up 8% over one month and 10% over six months, to €49. Buy ratings make up 23% of the total, four points more than three months ago. The dashboard's revision score of 15 is the best in the beverages sector, ahead of Diageo (11) and Campari (9), with Pernod Ricard at (7).

Narrative: split, and shifting from fundamentals to valuation. Bernstein, long the most constructive large broker, downgraded the shares to Market-Perform on 27 October 2026 because the rally "fairly reflects better times to come". Deutsche Bank notes that the multiple has expanded about ten times as fast as estimates. Individual target prices range from €35 to €80, and the median target is below the share price.

Technical momentum: strong but young, and the pinned grade is B (dashboard of 23 November 2026). The share price is 16.7% above its 200-day moving average and 6% below its 52-week high. It has risen 7% over three months, 28% over six and 34% over twelve, and its relative strength is at the 84th percentile. The 200-day average has risen in only four of the last twelve months, so the uptrend is young.

Peers: Rémy leads the spirits group on share price and on revisions. Diageo is also graded B on both readings (its shares are up 8% over twelve months); Campari is graded D and C, and Pernod Ricard D and F.

Inference: momentum is strong in level but thin in quality. The upgrades come from currency, the share price has outrun earnings, and the brokers who were bullish are stepping back on valuation. That pattern is typical of an early turn, and it leaves the shares exposed to one poor quarter.

The counter-case and what would change my view. Young uptrends with rising estimates often run further than valuation-minded brokers expect. A first upgrade driven by organic sales rather than currency would make the momentum of a better kind.

Against the market. I agree with the direction the share price shows, but differ on what the move has earned: a turn, not yet a broadening.

Conclusion: momentum is positive on every pinned reading and the best among spirits peers, but it rests on currency upgrades and a re-rating. Bearing on the case: momentum supports step 3 on the narrative turning, and weakens step 6, because part of the reward has already been collected.

Score: 84, set by the Rater. Both measures sit in the top fifth, but the narrative part is negative (Bernstein downgraded on valuation, the median target is below the price, only 23% Buy) and guidance was lifted only on currency and tariffs, so not every part is positive and the letter is B. Placed high in the band because revisions of +4%/+5%/+6% at one, three and six months are about 1.0 times revenue growth, the price is 16.7% above a newly rising 200-day average and the stock leads its spirits peers, held below A by revisions that are currency-driven rather than organic.

#9 Riskiness of the case

Simplicity: the case is not simple. It has six moving parts (two markets, two currencies, wholesaler stock, price-mix, tariffs, and savings net of reinvestment), and reported sales can mislead for a quarter or two in either direction.

Seven fragilities, from trade to people.

Suddenness, predictability and trackability: shocks can be sudden, but demand is unusually visible. Tariff and currency shocks are sudden: the shares fell 8.5% in a day on China tariff news in October 2024. Demand is trackable monthly through NABCA and Nielsen data and quarterly through sales releases, which is unusually good visibility for a cyclical business. Profit, however, is disclosed only twice a year.

Precedents: past recoveries were sharp, but they were led by price. Redburn counts eight downturns in cognac shipments since the 1950s and six downgrade cycles in three decades. In 2012-14, China's cognac volumes fell 22% and the group margin fell 340 basis points in a year, then recovered through price-mix and cost. Two things are different now: both big markets fell together, where one used to cushion the other, and price is falling, where past recoveries were led by price. Past cycles say that recoveries are sharp once stock is clear; they do not say what a recovery without price looks like.

Risks to the share price beyond the fundamentals. Rémy trades at a premium multiple to peers that sit at the bottom of their own ranges; a risk-off market would penalise its leverage and complexity; and the median broker target is below the share price.

The counter-case: the risks are many, but mostly visible and dated. The worst of them (a 38% duty and a covenant breach) have been removed in the last 18 months, and family control, with a hybrid in place, makes a forced outcome unlikely.

What would change my view. Leverage below 2.8 times before the hybrid by March 2027, and a second year under the China undertaking without incident, would move the case towards average risk.

Against the market: the live risk is the quiet one. The June Risks report recommended killing the case, and brokers' bear cases run to €22-26 a share. I think that tail is real, but less likely than it was in June. The live risk is quieter: a restock that looks like recovery while falling price-mix erodes the margin.

Conclusion: a complex case with above-average risk, whose worst outcomes have receded and whose main remaining risk can be tracked monthly. Bearing on the case: the risks weaken the certainty of steps 3 and 6, and they are why the three conditions in step 7 are framed around depletions and price-mix rather than reported sales.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. The memo's cone puts two-year-forward earnings 17% below to 13% above the base, the case has six moving parts (two markets, two currencies, wholesaler stock, price-mix, tariffs, savings net of reinvestment) on net debt/EBITDA of 3.5x (worse than 80% of the Universe), with sudden tariff and currency shocks, a reversible China undertaking, a distributor in Chapter 11, eight shipping downturns in the sector's history and bear cases near EUR 21-26; family control, the hybrid and monthly NABCA/Nielsen tracking cushion it. Several low-correlation drivers on a geared balance sheet place it below D'Ieteren's complex holding and just above Helios Towers' concentrated leveraged case.

#10 Lifecycle phase

The dashboard's rule places the stock in Broadening; on the evidence I would place it one notch earlier, turning up and at the door of Broadening.

For turning up. Organic growth has returned after two years of falls near 20%; estimates have stopped falling after four years of cuts; the share price is above a 200-day average that has only just begun to rise; and the dashboard's own stage reading is "early".

Not stalling or collapsing. Depletions are improving in both main markets, and the balance sheet has been repaired ahead of need.

Against Broadening, so far. A broadening thesis has more than one leg and wins converts. Here the upgrades have one source (currency), the growth comes from one division (cognac up, while liqueurs and spirits fell about 7%) and one region (Asia up 14%, the Americas and Europe down), and the most constructive large broker has just downgraded the shares. The US would be the second leg, and the US recovery has not yet shown in shipments.

So what: the phase sets the fair multiple (see #11). The guideline multiple for Broadening is the 80th percentile of the stock's own history, and a stock that is only turning up, with less certain forecasts, warrants less.

What would change my view. Americas sales turning positive and one upgrade driven by organic sales would make Broadening the right label; a negative third quarter beyond the China stock adjustment would make it a stall.

Against the market. The price action says Broadening; the sell-side's ratings say not yet. I side with the sell-side on the label and with the share price on the direction.

Conclusion: the stock is turning up, with Broadening one or two good results away. Bearing on the case: the phase supports step 2 on the direction of change, and weakens step 6 by pointing to a lower fair multiple than the guideline.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's early Turning up rather than the computed Broadening: organic growth has returned after two years near (20)%, estimates have stopped falling and the 200-day average has only just started rising, but the upgrades have one source (currency), the growth one division and one region, the US leg is not in shipments, a China destock is due in Q3, and the multiple has already moved from 15 to 23 times with the leading bull downgrading on valuation. A real but narrow early turn with part of the good news priced sits just below Kerry and above Nexans.

#11 Fair multiple

The guideline fair multiple is 32.48 times two-year forward earnings: the 80th percentile of the stock's ten-year history, set for the Broadening phase, and 43% above today's 22.65 times. Applied to today's two-year forward earnings per share of about €2.22, the guideline multiple gives a share price of about €72.

My view: the guideline multiple is too high for the evidence today, but it is not absurd.

Why the guideline is too high: it is drawn from eras when the business had pricing power. The ten-year history covers two different eras. From 2016 to 2019 the shares traded at 24-33 times while price-mix was positive, and from mid-2020 to the end of 2021 at 38-49 times in a boom. In the 50 months since September 2022 the multiple has not been above 25.1 times. The 80th percentile is therefore drawn entirely from a business with pricing power and returns on capital well above today's 7.7%. Spirits peers at 12-17 times, at the bottom of their own ranges, show that the market no longer pays those multiples for the category.

Why the guideline is not absurd: a multiple on trough earnings is a bet on normal earnings. At a 25% operating margin on FY29 sales, the company would earn about €3.00 a share, and €72 would be 24 times that figure. The guideline price therefore asks for two things together: an operating margin back in the mid-20s, and a mid-20s multiple on the earnings that margin produces. Each is plausible; both at once is the bull case.

What I would use: 24-27 times while the margin path is unproven (the ten-year median is 26.0 times), moving towards 30 times and above after two half-years of positive cognac price-mix and a stated margin objective above 22%. In the worse case the tenth percentile (18.6 times) is the reference, and the March 2025 low of 14.9 times is the stress point.

The counter-case. If Broadening is the right phase and estimates start rising for operating reasons, the multiple may overshoot, as multiples do in early recoveries; 30 times on rising earnings has precedent in this stock.

Against the market. At 22.6 times, the market already pays about the 30th percentile of the ten-year range, but near the top of the last two years' range. The market's multiple is closer to my view than to the guideline.

Conclusion: the guideline of 32.5 times is the multiple of a proven recovery, and I think 24-27 times fits the evidence in hand. Bearing on the case: the fair multiple weakens step 6, because most of the gap between a moderate and a large return is the multiple, not the earnings.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. Neutral on one and dear on the other gives D. The own-range reading flatters, because the ten-year history was built while the business had pricing power (the multiple has not exceeded 25 times since September 2022 and 22.6 times sits near the top of the last two years), but the premium partly reflects trough earnings and the memo's own fair multiple of 24-27 times is above today's, so I place it in the middle of the band.

#12 Total shareholder return

All returns start from today's share price of €50.35 and today's two-year forward earnings per share of €2.22 (consensus). My own forecasts put two-year forward earnings 3-4% lower, and the growth figures below already absorb that difference.

Over 12 months (to November 2027)
  • Earnings: two-year forward earnings per share rise to €2.40, +8%.
  • Dividend: €0.75, +1.5%.
  • At an unchanged multiple: about +9.5%. At the guideline multiple (+43%): about +56%.
Over 18 months (to May 2028)
  • Earnings: €2.53, +13.6%.
  • Multiple: unchanged at 22.65 times gives €57.2; the guideline 32.48 times gives €82.0, since 1.136 × 1.434 = 1.629.
  • Dividend: +1.5%.
  • Return: +15% at an unchanged multiple; +64% at the guideline multiple.
Over three years (to November 2029)
  • Earnings: €2.86 (assuming 8% growth in the year after my forecasts end), +28.5%, or 8.7% a year.
  • Multiple: unchanged gives €64.7; the guideline gives €92.8 (1.285 × 1.434 = 1.843).
  • Dividends: €0.75 + €0.90 + €1.05 = €2.70, +5.4%.
  • Return: +34% at an unchanged multiple (10% a year); +90% at the guideline multiple (24% a year); and +53% (15% a year) at 26 times, the ten-year median and the middle of my own range.

The probability-weighted return over 18 months is about +11%.

CaseProbabilityTwo-year forward earningsMultiplePriceReturn with dividend
Better: depletion-led restock, price-mix flat, about a quarter of the plan kept20%€2.8527 times€77+54%
Base: my forecasts, multiple unchanged45%€2.5322.65 times€57+15%

Weighted: 0.20 × 54% + 0.45 × 15% + 0.35 × (19)% = about +11% over 18 months, roughly 7% a year.

What drives the return: earnings and dividends supply about 10% a year, and the multiple supplies everything above that. Earnings growth supplies a dependable 8-9% a year if consensus is merely met. Dividends add about 1.5-2% a year, and there are no buybacks while reducing leverage comes first. The multiple will follow price-mix and the net value of RC Forward. I give the worse case more weight than the better case for three reasons: a single-pass analysis tends to flatter, the January sales release carries a known negative, and the shares have already risen 34% in a year.

The counter-case. If the guideline multiple is right, the base case alone returns 64% in 18 months, and the weighting above is far too cautious.

Against the market. The brokers' median target implies a small loss over 12 months. I am more positive than the brokers because I count the earnings growth they forecast but do not put in their targets, and I am less positive than the guideline.

Conclusion: a base return near 10% a year from earnings and dividends, a probability-weighted 11% over 18 months, and a much larger return only if the multiple re-rates. Bearing on the case: the return quantifies step 6, a moderately positive expected return with a wide range of outcomes, and upside that depends on proof that is two to four results releases away.

The Financial Analyst's model gives a lower return at the guideline multiple, from a different starting point. The model, calculated after this memo from the Analyst's forecast inputs, starts from a share price of €51.90 on 16 November 2026 and a two-year forward multiple of 26.5 times, and its horizons end on fixed dates. On that basis, the return at the guideline multiple is +49.4% to 30 September 2027 and +75.0% to 31 March 2029, with earnings the larger part of the return over three years. The model's full table and its notes are in Appendix B.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. About +11% gives C and maps to about 52; I place it at the floor of the band because the lower tail is fat (35% on (19)%, bears' floor near EUR 21-26) and the upside rests on a re-rating, while the three-year check (+34% at an unchanged multiple, about 10% a year, from earnings and dividends) is supportive enough to hold it in C.

#13 Summary conclusion

Rémy Cointreau is a good brand business at trough earnings, whose causes for concern are clearing on dated evidence, with a self-help plan to which consensus gives almost no net value, on a multiple that has already recovered half-way. The fundamentals are skewed to the upside; the shares, after a 34% rise, are roughly balanced. The difference between a return of 10% a year and a much better one is whether cognac price-mix stops falling and whether the savings are kept. Both questions will be answered within three to four results releases, and the data that settle them are monthly and public.

What to watch, in order.

Memo ratings. The four ratings below match the grades mapped from the earlier memo of August 2026, re-tested against the October evidence: the change forces have strengthened within their grade, and the riskiness has eased within its grade.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 60, set by the Rater. The input forces are positive but uneven: a mild external net positive (destocking, tariff and currency relief against falling price, topic 1 at 53) and a funded internal plan whose net value is unstated (topic 2 at 65), and they reach profits mainly through volume and cost while price-mix, the most geared line, is still falling. Forecast EPS growth of about 11% a year is only around the Universe median and recovers margins part of the way, so clearly positive inputs lifting profits to about median growth put it at 60.

Foundations' Robustness: 42, set by the Rater. Strong brands in a closed, barrier-protected industry (topic 3 at 50) are undermined by a weak financial profile (ROIC 3%, negative free cash flow, 3.5x leverage), a moat shallow where the profit swing sits, low predictability through stock-driven cycles, and a delivery record with a guidance cut and withdrawn targets inside three years (topic 4 at 44); three good prints since the reset do not yet offset that, so it sits below typical.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 63, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits 'CfC in quality cyclical at trough-on-trough': trough earnings (EPS about 70% below the FY23 peak), several named causes for concern clearing on dated evidence and a quantified self-help plan are present, while the multiple no longer being at a trough is price and does not count here. The fit is blurred by a current problem, cognac price-mix still falling, by quality that is strong in brands but mediocre in returns, and by no agreed normal to revert to, so it sits at the low end of Richard's 65-75 range for a major cause for concern clearing in a middling-quality business.

Case Riskiness: 33, set by the Rater. A complex case (topic 9 at 35): six moving parts, sudden and partly reversible tariff and currency risks, a cyclical industry with a glut and 3.5x leverage that doubles errors, and a premium multiple to peers as a share-price risk; family control, the hybrid and monthly demand data that can be tracked keep it off the bottom quarter's floor.
